backgroundImageAltText: Four-panel cross-section diagram of the four major plasma lipoprotein classes arranged by decreasing size: chylomicron, VLDL, LDL and HDL.

params.text: The largest and least dense lipoprotein (density < 0.95 g/mL). Assembled in the enterocyte with ApoB-48, its core is mostly dietary triacylglycerol. It acquires ApoC-II (activates lipoprotein lipase) and ApoE (for hepatic remnant uptake) from HDL in the blood. Carries dietary fat from gut to tissues via the lymph; remnants are cleared by the liver through the ApoE receptor.

Assembled in the liver with ApoB-100, rich in endogenous triacylglycerol from hepatic lipogenesis. Lipoprotein lipase (activated by ApoC-II) progressively removes triacylglycerol, converting VLDL → IDL → LDL. This is the liver's main vehicle for exporting triacylglycerol to peripheral tissues.

The end-product of VLDL catabolism, carrying mostly cholesteryl ester with ApoB-100 retained on its surface. Delivers cholesterol to tissues via the LDL receptor (which recognises ApoB-100). When retained and oxidised in the arterial intima, macrophage scavenger receptors take it up without limit, forming the foam cells that start atherosclerosis.

The smallest and densest lipoprotein, rich in protein (ApoA-I). Mediates reverse cholesterol transport: collects excess cholesterol from cells via ABCA1, esterifies it with LCAT (activated by ApoA-I), and delivers it to the liver via SR-BI or transfers it to VLDL/LDL via CETP. High HDL is cardioprotective.
